newsitem.title: USA: U.S. HRW wheat in mostly good shape - agronomists.
newsitem.headline: U.S. HRW wheat in mostly good shape - agronomists.

text.p: The U.S. hard red winter wheat crop was in mostly good shape, but agronomists warned Tuesday that current unseasonably warm weather could open the crop to problems later this spring.
Agronomists said wheat in most areas of Oklahoma and Kansas benefited from recent rain and snow, but western areas of those states still could use more moisture.

"The condition of most of our wheat has been ameliorated by the snow," said Jim Shroyer, extension agronomist at Kansas State University. "I'm not saying bumper crops or anything like that, but so far the moisture is fairly good."
Mark Hodges, executive director of the Oklahoma Wheat Commission and a soils expert by training, echoed Shroyer's assessment.

"We have good wheat conditions all over the state. We've got really good subsoil moisture, and then about 10 days or so ago we got a wet snow on top of that so now we've got really good surface moisture," Hodges said.
"We're still a long way from having it in the bin, but at the present time we're in good shape," he said.
Hodges estimated that at least 80 percent of Oklahoma's winter wheat crop was in good to excellent condition.
In the latest crop report released February 3, the Oklahoma Agricultural Statistics Service rated the state's wheat condition at five percent excellent, 69 good, 23 fair and three fair.
That compared to three percent excellent, 75 percent good, 21 fair and one percent poor at the beginning of January.
The most recent Kansas crop report rated the state's winter wheat condition at 10 percent excellent, 65 good, 22 fair and three poor.
That compared to 16 percent excellent, 66 good, 17 fair and one percent poor at the beginning of January.
Shroyer said wheat in southwest Kansas could be at risk if above-normal temperatures continue during the rest of February.

"We had some miserably cold weather in March last year, and if we have a warm February... and it gets cold again, we could have some wheat obviously breaking dormancy and be in major trouble depending on how low it gets," he said.
Agronomists said it normally takes at least five consecutive days of above-normal weather to coerce wheat out of dormancy.
Unseasonably warm temperatures graced the U.S. Plains Monday and Tuesday, but temperatures were expected to be a little cooler Wednesday, said Fred Gesser, chief meteorologist at Weather Express Inc.
Gesser said a cooldown would begin Friday, and that temperatures next week in the central Plains would likely be two to four degrees below normal.

Gesser said a storm system developing in the southwest United States would likely bring moderate to heavy rains later this week to non-wheat producing areas of Texas. Wheat-growing areas in the Texas Panhandle would receive 0.1 to 0.50 inch of rain. Oklahoma was expected to receive similar amounts, but Gesser said Kansas and Nebraska would likely see very little if any precipitation.
"The best rains should fall in Oklahoma and Texas," Gesser said.
